[spoiler=Tired]
Bayarma the Second opened her eyes and gazed at the ceiling of her bedroom. She was answered with a deafening silence, which did little to help her lousy mood. She gave a long groan before getting out of bed, slowly moving herself up and into her slippers. She walked over to her bedroom window and looked out into the distance, with the beautiful city of Shiganuur in her view. Shiganuur gazed back, reeling from nightly festivities that never seemed to fade even as the hours passed.

She was getting old. Quite old. As Mÿra IIs sister, she had been deeply involved in Alaqan politics ever since her older sister had taken the throne, acting as an advisor for her. After Mÿras resignation in 2008 due to social exhaustion and age, Bayarma II had taken the reins as Khagan of Alaqar up to the modern day. She was now 59 years old, and while that wasnt remarkably old for politician standards, she had also spent decades working in government roles to support her sister. She was tired. Quite tired.

Now, she merely thought, while staring at the Euphoric City. Was she willing to serve another year? Bayarma had one daughter: Sadryne, an adopted half-elf. Sadryne had proven interested enough in Alaqan governance that the question of whether she wanted power or not. And she had no question in her abilities, most definitely not. Sadryne, as most Alaqan monarchs before her had, studied abroad at the National University of Velvetel and specialized in law. Bayarma had no doubt in her abilities as a potential leader.

Bayarma sighed a long, drawn out breath and fixed her eyes over to the crown, sitting comfortably in a finely carved stand. It was a very beautiful crown, a crown built with silver with gold lining, richly decorated with emeralds that brightly shined from the windows reflection. A crown that had served Bayarmas ancestors since the 16th century, and one that is kept in highest shape and praise. Yet she looked at it with exhaustion and grimace.

She felt like eating something. Enough with staring at jewelry. Its time for breakfast.
[/spoiler]

[spoiler= The Old Nation of Toqastan
[sub]An Expansion Post[/sub]]

The Toqastani and Kazhevikstani peoples are ethnic brethren, sharing common ancestry, linguistic roots, and cultural traditions that trace back to the eastern continent of Shamat. For centuries, their ancestors lived as semi-nomadic clans and settled communities, bound together by kinship networks, religious authority, and regional trade. This shared heritage was violently disrupted in the mid-1800s, when Jazeran colonists pushed into Shamat, displacing indigenous populations and seizing land through force, treaties signed under duress, and systematic demographic replacement.

In the aftermath of this expansion, historic Toqastani territory was divided between the emerging states of Ostarev and Kazhevikstan. Newly drawn borders split families, clans, and religious institutions, leaving the Toqastani people politically fragmented and deeply vulnerable. Both governments viewed assimilation as necessary for long-term stability, but their approaches diverged sharply, producing very different outcomes.

Ostarev pursued a hardline policy of integration, pressuring Toqastani communities to adopt the Jazeran language, identity, and legal norms. Religious institutions were placed under strict regulation, traditional leadership structures were sidelined or dismantled, and cultural practices deemed separatist were discouraged or outright banned. Over time, these measures fostered deep resentment, as many Toqastani came to view assimilation not as inclusion, but as cultural annihilation imposed by the state.

Kazhevikstan adopted a softer, though still fundamentally assimilative, approach. The Kazhevik Government framed the Toqastani as long-lost kin, brothers and sisters returning to the fold of a shared civilization. While this narrative diluted Toqastani distinctiveness and encouraged gradual cultural convergence, it also allowed for greater local governance, religious autonomy, and limited cultural expression. In recent years, Kazhevik authorities have further moderated their policies, rolling back forced language programs and expanding regional self-administration. These reforms have significantly reduced tensions and undercut support for radical movements, though suspicion toward the central government remains.

The consequences of these divergent strategies are stark. In Ostarev, Toqastani regions remain persistent hotbeds of unrest. Armed resistance movements operate in the shadows, drawing support from communities that feel politically marginalized and culturally erased. Protests, sabotage, and insurgent attacks are common in certain districts, reinforcing a vicious cycle of repression, retaliation, and further alienation.

The election of President Simon Ovstrovsky briefly raised hopes for de-escalation. Ovstrovsky has publicly pledged to cool tensions between the Jazeran majority and the Toqa minority, framing reconciliation as essential to national unity. However, many observers regard these promises as little more than political pandering. Under his administration, the controversial Ostarevi Energy Security Auxiliary (OESA) has expanded its operations significantly.

Ovstrovsky does receive some credit for the passage of the Toqastan Recognition Bill, which formally recognizes the northern territories of the nation as the Toqastan Oblast. The bill grants the region the right to form a state government and manage certain internal affairs, but it stops short of granting the powers or legal status of a sovereign republic, such as the Republic of Karwin. Supporters argue that the legislation represents a meaningful first step toward repairing relations, while critics contend that it merely formalizes control without addressing the core grievances of autonomy, cultural preservation, and political self-determination.

The Ostarevi Energy Security Auxiliary, officially a private security contractor, is widely rumored to be funded and directed by the Ostarevi Government, though no definitive proof has been publicly produced. The organization has conducted multiple cross-border raids into Kazhevikstan, ostensibly targeting insurgent networks and supply routes. However, it has been accused of committing serious crimes against civilians, particularly within Toqa communities. Human rights groups allege that the OESA operates with near-total impunity, blurring the line between state security forces and deniable paramilitary units. Its primary areas of operation lie in the oil-rich regions of historic Toqastan in northern Ostarev, where energy infrastructure, population control, and counterinsurgency are closely intertwined.

In Kazhevikstan, radical Toqastani elements do exist, but they lack broad popular support. Many Toqastani there view gradual accommodation as preferable to open conflict, particularly as recent reforms have demonstrated a willingness by the Kazhevik Government to coexist rather than dominate outright. Still, among elders, clerics, and cultural activists alike, there remains a shared and lingering fear: that time itself may succeed where policy has not slowly dissolving Toqastani identity on both sides of the border, until resistance becomes irrelevant not through defeat, but through forgetting.

Kazhevikstans response to raids carried out by the Ostarevi Energy Security Auxiliary has, at times, been severe. In 2018, the Kazhevik Armed Forces launched a multiple-launch rocket system strike on the Ostarevi border village of Kylmon, killing 28 civilians. The strike was carried out in direct response to an OESA raid three days earlier, which sabotaged a Kazhevikstani oil field and resulted in the deaths of six workers and three border guardsmen.

The Kazhevik Government has since become one of the loudest international critics of the Ostarevi Energy Security Auxiliary. It has submitted intelligence dossiers, satellite imagery, and intercepted communications to international watchdog groups in an effort to prove that the OESA operates with direct support from the Ostarevi state. While some governments and organizations have accepted this evidence as credible, others have dismissed it as circumstantial or politically motivated. As a result, the issue of the OESA remains a persistent diplomatic flashpoint, fueling regional instability and threatening to draw both nations into a wider and more overt conflict.

This is an issue that is specific to the northern mainland Belorevan region, as Karwin and Kyratov both do not have a Toqastani minority. Kyratov does face struggles with the Kazhevikstani minority within the nation, much like Ostarev does with the Toqastani minority. The Republic of Karwin, an autonomous republic within the Republic of Ostarev, does not deal with many internal issues. Karwin is an ethnically homogenous nation with a shared culture and religion. This region is the newest to be integrated to Belorev coming just this year in 2027. However, it finds itself close to the hotbed region of Toqastan, which leads many to believe that the fighting may find a way to spread onto the island. This is a concern which has lead the government to found the Karwin National Guard. It is this force that will stand ready to combat the growing political violence in the nation. 

[/spoiler]
